questions.q: When Salesforce acts as a Service Provider, who issues the signing certificate used in the SAML trust relationship?
options: Neither side needs a certificate when Salesforce is the SP
The certificate is generated automatically by the user's browser
Salesforce issues it, exactly as when Salesforce is the IdP
The external identity provider issues it, and Salesforce uploads and trusts it
questions.explain: As the SP, Salesforce trusts an external IdP's authentication — so the external IdP issues the certificate, and Salesforce uploads it to validate incoming assertions.

questions.q: Why isn't simply having a valid SAML SSO Setting record enough to make SP-initiated SSO work for ordinary users?
options: An admin must also explicitly enable SAML as the active login method/default to actually redirect unauthenticated users to the external IdP
SAML SSO Settings only work for API integrations, never for the login page
The record must be re-created every 24 hours
It is enough; no further action is needed
questions.explain: Configuring the trust relationship (certificate, Issuer, login URL) is necessary but not sufficient — an admin has to separately enable SAML as the active login behavior for SP-initiated redirects to actually happen.

questions.q: What is the most common self-inflicted outage when configuring Salesforce as an SP?
options: Enabling My Domain too early
Forgetting to assign permission sets
Disabling the standard login page for all users, including admins, before confirming SSO is reliable — locking everyone out if the IdP has an outage
Setting too many OAuth scopes
questions.explain: If the standard login page is disabled for everyone, including admins, an IdP outage or misconfiguration leaves no way back in to fix the problem.

questions.q: What is a 'break-glass' admin account used for in this context?
options: A shared account used by all customer support agents
The account that owns all Connected Apps
Testing new Apex code in production
An account deliberately kept able to bypass SSO, used only to recover access during an SSO outage
questions.explain: A break-glass account is a deliberate safeguard: it can still log in without relying on the external IdP, specifically so an admin isn't locked out if SSO breaks.

questions.q: A user logs in via SP-initiated SSO through a trusted external IdP. What determines what that user can then do in Salesforce?
options: The user's Salesforce profile, permission sets, role, and sharing rules — unaffected by the login method
The scopes configured on the SAML SSO Setting record
Nothing; SP-initiated users get full admin access by default
Whatever access level the external IdP's admin console assigns
questions.explain: As emphasized throughout this course, SSO changes how a user authenticates, never what they're authorized to do — that's still governed entirely by Salesforce's own authorization model.
